zones.label: Column 1

Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription and notes are reviewer-authored, not a reproduction of the index.

lines.note: Continues Iibocu on f285: everyone's ears and eyes are startled, idiomatically everyone is astonished. The initial Fito is the word anticipated by f285's catchword, not a repeated catchword on this page.
Completes Todos with present or past astonishment. The printed alternatives and their tildes are retained rather than forcing one tense.
Jibun here means time or occasion; jibun toorai suru is the arrival of the appropriate time. This is a new entry aligned at the column margin, not an indented continuation.

runs.text: o tempo, ou hora de algũa couſa. ¶

lines.note: Explains the coming of the time or hour for something. Iibũ begins another Japanese example; its abbreviated nasal and tilde belong to the roman word, not an isolated italic vowel.
Completes jibun wo ukagoo, seeking a suitable time or opportunity. The caroned contracted verb is preserved rather than modernized to ukagau.
Jibun wo motte mairoozu says that the speaker will come at the proper time. The initial is I rather than OCR ſ; tẽ- begins the Portuguese time-word across the line break.
Completes tẽ-po and introduces sootoo no jibun, a suitable occasion. Tempo is wholly in the italic Portuguese apparatus; the OCR's isolated roman T was spurious.
Completes conueni-ente as a suitable time for doing something. The next example begins jibun haz-, whose continuation below describes acting out of season or at the wrong time.
Completes faz-zureni mono wo suru, doing something at an unsuitable time. The middle of algũa is abraded; the surviving letters and repeated local form support this reading rather than OCR algaa.

runs.text: fora de tẽpo, ou de horas determinadas, &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies doing it out of time or outside the appointed hours. Tẽpo retains the printed abbreviation tilde.
This jibun means oneself, not time. The example begins a declaration that an offering is the speaker's own gift.

runs.text: Eu offereço isto da minha parte.

lines.note: Gozaru closes the Japanese statement; the translation says the speaker offers this on his own behalf. The existing short-s st in isto is retained under the project's ligature policy.
Adds one's own capacity or ability as another sense of jibun. The paragraph mark introduces a semantic extension of the same entry.
Jibun ni kanawanu means being unable to accomplish something through one's own means. The Portuguese mi is physically divided from nhas without a visible hyphen.
Completes mi-nhas and explains inability by one's own strength or capacity. No hyphen is inserted into the canonical preceding row.

runs.text: Tempo, ou conjunção em que ha

lines.note: Jibungara is a time characterized by particular circumstances. The Portuguese begins a definition of an occasion on which something notable occurs.

runs.text: algũa couſa notauel como tempo de peſte, ou de

lines.note: Specifies a notable circumstance, such as a period of plague. The second example of a troubled period continues below.
Persecution completes the list of circumstances illustrating jibungara. This short line closes the entry before the next headword.
Jikai concerns an admonition or rule one observes oneself, as mizukara imashime indicates. Prohi- begins the Portuguese alternative prohibition.
Completes prohi-bição and specifies a prohibition that someone keeps or observes, not merely an order imposed without observance.
Jikkai means ten precepts, directly matched by too no imashime and ten laws. The nasal abbreviation in mã- belongs to the divided Portuguese word below.
Completes mã-damentos, commandments. This does not identify a particular religious list beyond what the entry itself supplies.
Jichi is knowing for oneself, explicitly mizukara shiru. The following water example distinguishes firsthand experience from report.
The example says that on drinking water one knows its coldness or warmth oneself. The circumflex in printed nôde is retained rather than replacing it with an expected nasal spelling.

runs.text: o que bebe a agoa diſcerne ſe he fria, ou quẽte.

lines.note: Only the person drinking the water can tell whether it is cold or hot. Quẽte preserves the abbreviated nasal, and agoa retains the historical Portuguese spelling.

runs.text: i, o que experimenta, eße ſabẽ das couſas mais

lines.note: The explanatory i says that the person with experience knows more about things. The short curved mark in ſabè is retained as a grave from the aligned reading, although a damaged tilde is also possible; it is not normalized away on grammatical grounds.
Completes the comparison: firsthand experience teaches more than hearing about something. The historical ouuir spelling remains unchanged.
Iichi iqi is given as a name for Japan. The first character is I, not long s, and the gloss's tilde is over final o in Iapaõ.
Jichimena, also illustrated with hito, describes a serious and trustworthy person. Latin l introduces the alternative expression rather than a Japanese syllable.
Completes the characterization as upright and truthful. These qualities explain graue as seriousness or dignity, not physical weight.
Jichina mono and jichina hito similarly describe a serious person. Both Japanese alternatives are printed on this physical row.
Completes the gloss as straightforward and truthful. In this context ſimples is lack of duplicity, not a diagnosis or a claim about intelligence.

runs.text: Iichinimo nai mono. i, Iichino nai.

lines.note: The phrases describe someone without sincerity or seriousness, the opposite of Iichina. The tightly inked i+n in Iichino can resemble m or transposed ni; enlargement shows the dot over the first stem, favoring Iichino. The print remains locally difficult.
Completes cõ-trario de, opposite of Iichina. Iichina is an upright Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is therefore a typeface-review term.

runs.text: Iichiraxij. l, Iichina mono. vt Mono mǒſu

lines.note: Jichirashii describes the appearance of sincerity or seriousness, compared with jichina mono. The locally upright lowercase vt is preserved; the example begins with one's way of speaking.
Completes the example: even the manner of speaking seems sincere or dignified. Portuguese pa continues as rece without a visible line-end hyphen.
Completes pa-rece, saying that the speaker appears to possess dignity and truthfulness. This explains the appearance nuance of the Japanese adjective.
Jichoo is equated with bumaru, a porter or carrier. The Portuguese mariola is clarified by the description of carrying goods below; it is not assigned a modern pejorative sense here.
Describes someone who carries goods or baggage. Fato is material belongings in this gloss, and the short line completes the porter definition.
Jichuu means within a temple, directly explained as tera no uchi. The Portuguese supplies temple and monastery as alternatives.
Completes the monastery alternative. The printed moeſteiro vowel order is retained rather than modernized to mosteiro.
This jichuu is an explanatory annotation on a character, not a temple interior. The small mark over u appears caroned on reinspection; the Japanese phrase ji wo shirusu clarifies the gloss.
Specifies the object of the explanation or commentary: a written character. The tilde remains over u in algũa.
Jiko means oneself, given with mizukara and onore and translated as I myself. Initial v in vonore is retained as a historical positional spelling.
Jikoku is a time or hour, explained through toki and kizami. Iico- begins the first Japanese example on the next physical row.
Completes jikoku ga utsuru, the passing of the hour or time. The printed Paßarſe form is retained without normalizing its double-s representation.
A second example, jikoku toorai suru, describes the arrival of the hour. This final row is body text, not a catchword or signature.
This jikoku is one's own country, explicitly mizukara no kuni, distinct from time in the preceding column. Its Portuguese gloss continues with the country where one is situated.

runs.text: ou reino onde hum eſtà. Vt,

lines.note: Adds the country where one is currently living. The example contrasts jikoku with takoku, other countries; the visible t in taco- corrects the OCR's caco-.
Completes taco-cu and translates the pair as this and other kingdoms. The row is an indented continuation, not a new unindented entry.

runs.text: Ver o ſenhor, ou capitão na guerra as

lines.note: Jikken here is a lord's or commander's inspection of enemy heads in war. This is a historical definition, not the modern experiment sense of the same pronunciation.

runs.text: cabeças dos inimigos q̃ os ſeus cortarão. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies the heads taken by the commander's own men and introduces an example. Q̃ remains unexpanded; cortarão is retained as the printed verbal form.
Kubi wo jikken saseraruru illustrates the respectful construction for inspecting the heads. The Japanese example has no additional Portuguese translation on this row.
Jikkyoo is true teaching, explicitly makoto no oshie. The Portuguese has doctri-, not OCR dostri-, beginning doctrine across the line boundary.
Completes doctri-na verdadeira, true doctrine. The adjective applies to the teaching just defined.
Jikkin describes closeness or intimacy, matched by mutsumashii and chikashi. Familiar begins the Portuguese pair of equivalents.
Priuado completes the sense as an intimate or close associate. It should not automatically be given the modern privacy-related sense.
Jikun means two lords, explicitly futari no kimi. The following maxim concerns serving two masters.
The maxim says that an exemplary retainer does not serve two lords. In- begins the Portuguese characterization of that person as distinguished.

runs.text: ſigne, & aprimorado não ſerue a dous ſe-

lines.note: Completes in-ſigne and describes an accomplished man who does not serve two lords. Se- begins ſenhores on the next row.
Completes ſe-nhores, the two masters in the translated maxim. This is a short body continuation.
Jidai is an age or period, matched by toki and yo and Portuguese idade. The definition concerns time, not a person's numerical age specifically.

runs.text: Modo de piſar cõ os pees. Vt,

lines.note: Jidanda is a manner of stamping or treading with the feet. The scan prints pees with two e letters; Ii- starts jidanda in the example below.
Completes jidanda wo fumu, stamping one's feet. Vide introduces the reference Fumi, u.; this is an upright Japanese cross-reference within Portuguese apparatus, not another independent headword.
Jidaraku and its adjectival form describe someone careless or disorderly. The Portuguese begins with desmazelado; the printed comma after the headword is retained.
Adds disorderliness, then exemplifies a careless person. Ho begins homem on the next physical row; no terminal hyphen is visible, and both letters are italic.
Completes Ho-mem and describes a person careless about arranging things. The visible hyphen after concer- belongs to the division of concertar.

runs.text: tar, & por por ordem as couſas, &c.

lines.note: Completes concertar and describes putting things in order. The two occurrences of por are retained: the first is the verb meaning put, the second the preposition in por ordem.
Jidō is glossed with chigo and historical varanbe, a child. Minino is the printed Portuguese spelling and is not modernized to menino.
Jidoku means reading for oneself, explicitly mizukara yomu. The example below concerns learning a book without a teacher.

runs.text: Cono qiǒ xixǒ nǒte tada jidocu, itaita.

lines.note: The speaker says that he read or learned this book independently, without a master. The carons and the small comma after jidocu are retained as printed, rather than normalizing the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Eſte liuro ſem meſtre ſò por mi o aprẽdi, ou lî.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as learning or reading this book by oneself without a master. The abbreviation in aprẽdi is retained; the tiny marks near so and final li are not expanded into conjectural accents.
Jihi denotes compassion, mercy, or almsgiving. The scan supports Miſericordia, not the OCR's Muſericordia; Iifiuo begins the Japanese example.
Completes jihi wo moppara to suru, making charitable giving a principal concern. Neceßa continues into ria without a visible terminal hyphen.
Completes neceßaria and identifies giving alms as a necessary, principal undertaking. Principal is one word in the scan; the next example begins after the pilcrow.
The alternatives jihi wo taruru and jihi wo suru are glossed as giving alms. The final Iifi starts the contrasting example about receiving charity.
Completes jihi wo ukuru, receiving alms. This is the continuation of the previous example, not a new entry.

runs.text: Eſmoler, ou amigo de fazer eſmolas.

lines.note: Jihijin is a charitable person, explained as an almsgiver or someone fond of giving alms. The f-like letter in the historical romanization is retained consistently with Iifi.

runs.text: Couſa de eſmola, ou peßoa eſmoler.

lines.note: Jihi na describes something charitable or a person who gives alms. The Portuguese expressly allows both a thing and a person as referent.

runs.text: Letra da propria mão, ou couſa eſcrita

lines.note: Jihitsu means one's own handwriting or something written by one's own hand. The printed headword Iifit is kept rather than completing it to a modern romanization.
Completes the explanation of autograph writing as something written by the person's own hand. This belongs to Iifit, not to the charitable-giving entries around it.

runs.text: Homem eſmoler, ou amigo de fazer

lines.note: Jihisha is a charitable person, here an almsgiver or someone who likes giving alms. The Portuguese definition continues on the next row.
Completes fazer eſmolas, giving alms. The isolated word is a body continuation rather than a catchword.
Jihishin is a compassionate heart, explicitly jihi no kokoro. The Portuguese piadoſo has the sense of merciful or compassionate in this context.
Jihishin wo okosu means arousing compassion. The gloss describes being moved to pity; the initial pilcrow introduces the example.
Adds mercy as an equivalent to pity in the preceding example. The spelling miſericordia is retained without modern accentuation.

runs.text: Homem de bem fazer, ou eſmoler.

lines.note: Jihishin na describes a benevolent or charitable person. Bem fazer is printed as two words and is not joined into a modern lexical form.
Jihiya denotes a charitable house or hospital. The apparent b in the OCR is the italic h of hoſpital; the institutional Portuguese expression is retained as printed.
Jihō means the rules of a temple or monastery, explicitly tera no hatto. The printed Portuguese vowel order moesteiro is retained; it is not modernized to mosteiro.
Jihō wo tamotsu means observing the monastery's rules. The Portuguese translation continues with the institution on the next row.
Completes the phrase about keeping the convent's rules. Conuento is the historical spelling of convento and is not a separate headword.
Jifu means a compassionate father, matched by itsukushimu chichi. The historical spellings Itçucuximu and Pay are preserved.

Jiga and jigabachi name a kind of stinging insect, described here as a kind of bee. The initial is capital I, not long s; the historical Portuguese classification is not silently changed to a modern zoological one.

Jiga wa noki ni su wo kakuru describes those insects building a nest under the eaves. The scan reads Iigaua and ſuuo, not OCR Iigana and ſiuo. Aquellas abe- continues into the next page; the separate italic footer lhas is its catchword.
